mcqs.q: The three postoperative complications of exodontia are:
opts: Bleeding, delayed healing and infection, and alveolar osteitis
Oroantral communication, tuberosity fracture and trismus
mcqs.explain: These are the complications arising after the extraction, as distinct from the operative complications arising during it.

mcqs.q: Bleeding (haemorrhage) is defined as:
opts: The escape of the blood outside the vascular system
A fall in the circulating platelet count
Failure of a clot to form within 24 hours
Any loss of more than 500 mL of blood
mcqs.explain: The definition is about blood leaving the vessels, not about volume or platelet count.

mcqs.q: Primary haemorrhage occurs:
opts: At the time of the operation or accident
Within the first 24 hours after control
mcqs.explain: Primary bleeding is the bleeding of the operation itself.

mcqs.q: Intermediary bleeding occurs:
opts: Within the first 24 hours, after the primary bleeding was controlled
At the moment of the extraction itself, before any pack
After the first postoperative day has already passed
Only when a systemic bleeding disorder is present
mcqs.explain: It is the early rebleed once the initial bleeding has already been stopped.

mcqs.q: Secondary haemorrhage may occur as late as:
mcqs.explain: Secondary haemorrhage arises any time after the first postoperative day and may appear up to two weeks later.

mcqs.q: Besides timing, bleeding may also be classified as:
opts: External or internal, and arterial, venous or capillary
Acute or chronic, with no further subdivision
Mild, moderate or severe by the volume lost
Local or referred, depending on where it is felt
mcqs.explain: Three axes are used: timing, site, and the vessel involved.

mcqs.q: Which is a LOCAL cause of postoperative bleeding?
opts: Interference by the patient with the formed clot
Haemophilia B, a specific factor defect
mcqs.explain: The other three are systemic disorders of platelets or clotting factors.

mcqs.q: Improper instructions for the use of pressure packs is classified as:
mcqs.explain: It is a fault at the wound, not in the patient's clotting mechanism.

mcqs.q: A nutrient canal is:
opts: A bony canal in the alveolar bone containing nutrient vessels
A channel in the pulp chamber
A space between the root and the socket wall
An accessory canal in the root apex
mcqs.explain: Bleeding from a severed, relatively large vessel running in such a canal is a recognised local cause.

mcqs.q: A retained root left in the socket may cause bleeding because:
opts: The clot fails to form over a severed vessel in its root canal
It raises the blood pressure locally
mcqs.explain: The vessel in the root canal keeps bleeding because no clot forms on top of it.

mcqs.q: Systemic bleeding may be due to a defect in:
mcqs.explain: These are the three systemic families of cause.

mcqs.q: Thrombocytopenic purpura means the platelets are:
mcqs.explain: Cytopenic means a reduced count; the functional defect is thrombocytopathic and the excess is thrombocythemia.

mcqs.q: Thrombocytopathic purpura means the platelets:
mcqs.explain: The count may be normal; it is the function that fails.

mcqs.q: Thrombocythemia (thrombocytosis) means the platelets are:
mcqs.explain: Paradoxically an excessive platelet count can also present with bleeding.

mcqs.q: Haemophilia exists in which forms?
mcqs.explain: The lecture lists haemophilia A, B and C.

mcqs.q: Pseudohaemophilia is also called:
mcqs.explain: Pseudohaemophilia is the vascular form.

mcqs.q: Which is a disease involving a specific blood factor?
mcqs.explain: Fibrinogen is a clotting factor; the others are platelet or vessel problems.

mcqs.q: Defects of the blood vessels causing bleeding may be:
mcqs.explain: Both forms are recognised.

mcqs.q: Which acquired factor increases the liability to bleed?
mcqs.explain: The liver makes most clotting factors, so severe liver disease produces a coagulation defect.

mcqs.q: Which drug group is listed among the commonest causes of increased bleeding?
mcqs.explain: Aspirin, anticoagulants, some chemotherapeutics, prolonged antibiotics and alcohol are the common offenders.

mcqs.q: Prolonged antibiotic therapy can increase bleeding because it:
mcqs.explain: It is listed among the drugs that interfere with coagulation.

mcqs.q: Management of postoperative bleeding is divided into how many phases?
mcqs.explain: Psychogenic shock, diagnosis, then treatment.

mcqs.q: Phase I of management is:
opts: Prevention and management of psychogenic shock
mcqs.explain: The patient is reassured before the cause is hunted.

mcqs.q: Psychogenic shock in these patients arises mainly from:
opts: Apprehension at blood filling the mouth and staining the clothes
The volume of blood actually lost
mcqs.explain: It is a fear response, not a volume response.

mcqs.q: If a patient bleeds for a long time without treatment, he may develop:
mcqs.explain: Rarely, prolonged untreated bleeding progresses from fear to true volume loss.

mcqs.q: What can PREVENT the development of psychogenic shock?
opts: The dentist's manner in receiving and reassuring the patient
Packing the socket with iodoform gauze
mcqs.explain: Assuring the patient that the condition will be controlled is itself the preventive measure.

mcqs.q: The first diagnostic step in Phase II is to determine:
opts: The tendency of the blood to clot
The exact volume of blood lost
mcqs.explain: It can be judged roughly by visual examination of the blood in the mouth.

mcqs.q: Blood in the mouth that shows a tendency to clot suggests:
mcqs.explain: A normal clotting mechanism points the search towards the wound itself.

mcqs.q: Blood with a fluidy character and no clotting tendency suggests:
opts: A coagulation defect and systemic deficiency
Interference with the clot by the patient
mcqs.explain: The clotting mechanism itself is disturbed.

mcqs.q: Bleeding from a soft tissue laceration is corrected by:
opts: Crushing spongy bone into the point
mcqs.explain: The other measures address bleeding from the bony socket.

mcqs.q: Bleeding from a nutrient canal can be stopped by:
opts: Bone wax, or crushing spongy bone into the bleeding point
Suturing the overlying gingiva by itself
Curetting the whole socket to fresh bone
mcqs.explain: The canal must be sealed mechanically.

mcqs.q: Before dismissing a patient whose bleeding has been controlled, the operator must:
opts: Examine him after 15 minutes and confirm no more bleeding
Keep him for a full 24 hours
mcqs.explain: A new pressure pack is then applied and the routine instructions given.

mcqs.q: A patient with a suspected coagulation disorder should be:
mcqs.explain: Local measures alone will not stop bleeding caused by a systemic defect.

mcqs.q: Which laboratory test is used in determining the responsible disorder?
mcqs.explain: Bleeding time, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time and clotting time are the ones listed.

mcqs.q: Applying ice to the region helps haemostasis by:
mcqs.explain: Cold constricts the vessels and so reduces flow.

mcqs.q: Which is a local haemostatic agent?
mcqs.explain: Absorbable gelatin sponge, oxidized cellulose, thrombin and collagen are the agents listed.

mcqs.q: In bleeding due to a systemic disorder, local measures alone will:
opts: Not stop the bleeding without correcting the deficient factor
Stop it only if ice is added
Stop it only if the socket is sutured
mcqs.explain: The defective or deficient factor must be corrected.

mcqs.q: Delayed healing is a rare complication following:
opts: Any extraction of a third molar
mcqs.explain: It is rare after simple extraction but may occur after surgical extraction, mostly due to infection.

mcqs.q: Infection after oral surgical procedures is prevented by:
opts: Careful asepsis and good wound debridement
mcqs.explain: Technique, not drugs, is the stated preventive measure.

mcqs.q: Alveolar osteitis is a condition in which:
opts: The clot disintegrates, leaving the socket bare of granulation tissue
The socket fills with excessive granulation tissue
The alveolar bone fractures during extraction
mcqs.explain: The bare bone is what produces the severe pain.

mcqs.q: The pain of dry socket mostly starts on the:
opts: Third or fourth day after the extraction
mcqs.explain: The clot forms first and is then lysed, which is why the pain is delayed.

mcqs.q: Dry socket is more common:
opts: In the mandible, especially after impacted third molars
In the maxilla, especially after anterior teeth
mcqs.explain: Impacted mandibular third molars are the classic setting.

mcqs.q: The dry socket appears to be due to:
opts: Increased fibrinolytic activity lysing the clot
Bacterial invasion of the bone marrow
Failure of the clot to ever form
mcqs.explain: The exact aetiology is unknown, but fibrinolysis of the formed clot is the accepted explanation.

mcqs.q: Which is a predisposing factor for dry socket?
mcqs.explain: Pre-existing infection or inflammation and excessive trauma are the two listed factors.

mcqs.q: In managing dry socket, the socket should be:
opts: Gently irrigated with saline, avoiding curettage
Thoroughly curetted to fresh bleeding bone
mcqs.explain: Curetting re-traumatizes the bare bone; only debris and lysed clot remnants are removed.

mcqs.q: The socket is packed with iodoform gauze saturated with a medication containing:
mcqs.explain: The dressing is to relieve pain and keep the area clean while the socket heals.

mcqs.q: The dressing procedure for dry socket is repeated:
opts: Daily or every other day for two or three days
Every hour for the first day
mcqs.explain: The frequency depends on the severity of the pain.

mcqs.q: Once the pain of dry socket decreases, the socket should be:
opts: Left without dressing to heal normally
Dressed for a further two weeks
mcqs.explain: The aim throughout is to relieve pain and let it heal naturally.

mcqs.q: Regarding antibiotics in dry socket:
opts: They have no role in its management
mcqs.explain: Dry socket is clot lysis, not infection, so antibiotics are not indicated in most cases.

saqs.q: Define bleeding and classify it by timing.
saqs.a: BLEEDING (haemorrhage) is the escape of the blood outside the vascular system. BY TIMING — PRIMARY occurs at the time of the operation or accident; INTERMEDIARY occurs within the first 24 hours, after the primary bleeding has been controlled; SECONDARY occurs any time after the first postoperative day and may occur as late as two weeks postoperatively.

ans.text: The escape of the blood outside the vascular system.

head: Type
When it occurs
rows: at the time of the operation or accident
within the first 24 hours, after the primary bleeding has been controlled
any time after the first postoperative day — as late as two weeks postoperatively

ans.text: It may also be classified as external or internal, and as arterial, venous or capillary.

saqs.q: List the local causes of postoperative bleeding.
saqs.a: A. Interference by the patient with the formed clot. B. Improper instructions for the use of the pressure packs. C. Soft tissue lacerations. D. Failure of the blood clot to form on top of a severed vessel in the root canal of a retained root left in the socket. E. The presence of a nutrient canal in the wall of the bony socket, with failure of the clot to form on the severed, relatively large vessel running in it.

list: A. Interference by the patient with the formed clot
B. Improper instructions for the use of the pressure packs
D. Failure of the clot to form over a severed vessel in the root canal of a retained root left in the socket
E. A nutrient canal in the socket wall, the clot failing to form on the severed, relatively large vessel running in it

ans.text: Nutrient canals are bony canals in the alveolar bone that contain nutrient vessels.

saqs.q: Classify the systemic causes of bleeding.
saqs.a: Bleeding may be due to a defect in platelets, a coagulation disorder, or a defect in the vessels. A) PLATELET DISEASE — thrombocytopenic purpura, thrombocytopathic purpura, thrombocythemia. B) SPECIFIC BLOOD FACTORS — haemophilia A, B or C; pseudohaemophilia (vascular haemophilia); parahaemophilia; hypofibrinogenaemia; hypoprothrombinaemia. C) DEFECTS OF BLOOD VESSELS, congenital or acquired.

saqs.q: Which acquired factors increase the liability to bleeding?
saqs.a: Severe liver diseases, elevated blood pressure, and drugs that interfere with the coagulation process — the most common being aspirin, anticoagulants, some chemotherapeutic drugs, prolonged antibiotic therapy and alcohol use.

saqs.q: Give the three phases of managing postoperative bleeding, and what happens in Phase I.
saqs.a: PHASE I — prevention and management of psychogenic shock. PHASE II — diagnosis and looking for the cause. PHASE III — treatment. In PHASE I, the apprehension of the patient at blood filling his mouth and colouring his clothes may cause fear and psychogenic shock, and rarely hypovolaemic shock if bleeding continues untreated. The dentist's behaviour in receiving the patient can prevent it, by assuring him the condition will be controlled.

head: Phase
What it covers
rows: diagnosis — looking for the cause of the bleeding

ans.text: Phase I — apprehension at blood filling the mouth, sometimes staining the clothes, may cause fear and psychogenic shock; rarely, prolonged untreated bleeding brings on hypovolaemic shock. The dentist's manner in receiving the patient prevents it, by assuring him the condition will be controlled.

saqs.q: How is the cause of the bleeding diagnosed from the blood in the patient's mouth?
saqs.a: The first step is to find the tendency of the blood to clot, demonstrated roughly by visual examination of the blood in the patient's mouth. If there IS a tendency to clot, the clotting mechanism is normal and the cause is likely local. If the blood has a fluidy character with no clotting tendency, the clotting mechanism is disturbed by a coagulation defect and systemic deficiency. If local, the operator must then determine whether it comes from the soft tissues or the bony socket.

head: Appearance of the blood
Interpretation
rows: clotting mechanism is normal — the cause is likely LOCAL
clotting mechanism is disturbed — a coagulation defect and systemic deficiency

ans.text: If the cause is local, the operator next determines whether the bleeding comes from the soft tissues or from the bony socket.

saqs.q: How is bleeding from a local cause treated?
saqs.a: SOFT TISSUE LACERATION — corrected by adequate suturing. BONY SOCKET with a root fragment — remove the fragment and give routine postoperative instructions. BONY SOCKET with a nutrient canal — seal it with bone wax, or crush spongy bone into the bleeding point with the tip of a blunt instrument. INTERFERENCE WITH THE CLOT — pressure packs and proper instructions. The operator must not dismiss the patient until he has examined him after 15 minutes and found no more bleeding, then applied a new pressure pack.

head: Source
Treatment
rows: remove the fragment, then routine postoperative instructions
seal with bone wax, or crush spongy bone into the bleeding point with a blunt instrument tip

ans.text: Important — do not dismiss the patient until he has been examined after 15 minutes and shows no more bleeding; a new pressure pack is then applied with the routine instructions.

saqs.q: Define alveolar osteitis and outline its management.
saqs.a: ALVEOLAR OSTEITIS (dry socket) is a condition in which the blood clot disintegrates and leaves the bony socket bare of granulation tissue, resulting in severe pain. It starts on the third or fourth day, is commoner in the mandible especially after impacted third molars, and appears to be due to increased fibrinolytic activity lysing the clot. MANAGEMENT aims to relieve pain and let the socket heal naturally: irrigate gently with saline avoiding curettage; dry and isolate; pack loosely with iodoform gauze saturated with a sedative and antiseptic medication; repeat daily or every other day for two or three days. Once pain decreases leave it undressed; give an analgesic; antibiotics have no role.

ans.text: A condition in which the blood clot disintegrates and leaves the bony socket bare of granulation tissue, resulting in severe pain.

rows: the third or fourth day after extraction
commoner in the mandible, especially after impacted third molars
increased fibrinolytic activity lysing the clot and exposing the bone

ans.h: Management — relieve pain, let it heal naturally
steps: Irrigate gently with saline, avoiding curettage — remove only debris and lysed clot remnants
Dry the socket gently and isolate the area
Pack loosely with iodoform gauze saturated with a sedative and antiseptic medication
Repeat daily or every other day for two or three days, depending on the pain
Once the pain decreases, leave it without dressing to heal normally

ans.text: An analgesic may be prescribed; antibiotics have no role, since dry socket is clot lysis rather than infection.
